To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) when the costs of making errors are low, agents evolve to use trivial (but optimal), strategies; (b) when costs are higher, agents evolve to make decisions based on a heuristic strategy, and (c) when the costs are high and the information is of low quality, agents evolve to employ an optimal strategy, but only if they have enough cognitive resources to do so.

1) optimal decision strategies evolve in the presence of high quality information, 2) heuristics evolve as a response to high cognitive demands, 3) heuristics and optimal strategies are both found to be optimal in different contexts, 4) the optimal strategies that evolve are not the ones predicted by the optimal decision-making literature, and 5) heuristics can evolve to perform optimally in some contexts.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the evolution of optimal strategies is a function of task difficulty and punishment magnitude, and the evolution of heuristic strategies is a function both of task difficulty and of punishment magnitude.

the optimal decision-making strategy evolves in the presence of high information quality and low punishment magnitudes, whereas the heuristics evolve under the opposite conditions, and that the heuristics are a response to the high cognitive demands imposed by the decision task.
the evolutionary process is not only able to find optimal strategies, but also to develop heuristics in cases where optimal strategies are too difficult to achieve.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

optimal decision-making strategies evolve under conditions where information quality is high or punishment magnitude is low, but heuristic strategies evolve under conditions that are more demanding on cognitive resources.

the evolution of optimal strategies is favored by environments that provide high quality information, and the evolution of heuristics is favored by environments where the quality of information is poor and where the cost of errors is high.
heuristics and optimality are not mutually exclusive, and that both can evolve in the face of the same environmental conditions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
optimal decision-making strategies are not the default, but rather a product of specific environmental conditions.
the evolution of decision strategies depends on the interaction between task demands and available cognitive resources.

optimal and heuristic strategies are not fixed properties of a task, but instead are the result of the evolutionary history of the agents who perform the task, and the characteristics of the environment in which they live.
